title: Work as practice
hookLine: a task done with attention is practice
carry: fully there for the warm water and the plate

cards: Before he ever cooked for monks, he was a footman, and by his own account a great clumsy fellow who broke everything.

Later, as a lay brother in a Paris monastery, he was sent to the kitchen, work he says he naturally disliked. A few weeks ago, at the start of this block, this path met him there, in the clatter: Brother Lawrence.
Now, something smaller he said, about an egg in a pan, and about what to do when the mind wanders off. Today: samu.

teach.h: A LITTLE OMELET, FOR THE LOVE OF GOD.
teach.b: First, the omelet. Brother Lawrence's letters and conversations were gathered into a small book, The Practice of the Presence of God.
In paraphrase, he says we needn't do great things: he turns his little omelet in the pan for the love of God. The size of the task isn't the point.
And when he notices he has wandered, he doesn't scold himself or make a show of being sorry. He simply comes back. Second, the monastery work period.
In Zen monasteries in Japan, there's a name for the hours spent sweeping, weeding, cleaning and cooking: samu, work practice. It isn't a break from meditation.
It is meditation, with a broom. The attention given to the breath on a cushion is given to the corner of the floor. Third, the dishes.

The Vietnamese Zen teacher Thich Nhat Hanh wrote about washing dishes. In paraphrase: there are two ways to wash the dishes. One is to wash them to get them clean, so you can get on to the next thing.

teach.h: WASH THE DISHES TO WASH THE DISHES.
teach.b: The other is to wash the dishes to wash the dishes, fully there for the warm water and the plate in your hand. Only the second, he said, is really being alive while you do it. Fourth, what makes a task practice.
Not the task. A Christian cook, a Zen monastery and a Vietnamese teacher each speak from their own tradition, and each points at attention.
Any task, done with full attention and coming back when you drift, can become practice.
These weeks have asked why we work, and who for. This is about how.

how: In Zen monasteries, monks and visitors do samu, a period of cleaning, gardening and kitchen work done in silence as meditation; Christians drawn to Brother Lawrence try to keep God in mind through ordinary tasks.

games.q: you're Brother Lawrence. your mind has wandered off while turning the omelet. what do you do?
o: scold yourself and start the prayer again.
leave the kitchen for the chapel.
games.why: he simply comes back. the coming back, again and again, is the practice.

practice: For now, the breath is the task: follow it in and out, the way Brother Lawrence turned the omelet, just this one, now.
When the mind drifts to something else, notice where it went and come back, without scolding, then come back again. The coming back is the whole exercise.

wordCard.voice: Samu. The Zen name for work practice: sweeping, weeding and cooking done with the same attention given to the breath. Today's word.
